opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a funny one. I was reading it to my daughter, and the story is presented as an unambiguous triumph. There's this untouched wilderness, the animals build a road through it, put up a factory, and everyone is delighted. The book is a celebration of industry and progress, which makes sense for when it was written.

Reading it now, I had two reactions at once. One was a little wince. Many of us now read a story like that and immediately think about habitat loss, pollution, and what's being paved over. It struck me how much our moral intuitions about nature have shifted within a single lifetime. Something that was obviously good to one generation looks at least questionable to the next.

The other reaction, which I think is the more interesting one, was that I didn't want to just sneer at it. There's something genuinely admirable in that worldview. Building things lifted billions of people out of poverty. Roads connect people, and factories make the goods that let people live longer, healthier lives. The book captures a real optimism about human agency, the sense that we can shape the world and make it better. I think we've partly lost that, and in some quarters it has swung into a reflexive suspicion of building anything.

So I'd like a synthesis of the two. Keep that confidence that humanity can do great things and that progress is real and worth celebrating, but add the wisdom to ask what we're giving up, which costs are hidden, and which costs are irreversible. That's close to how I think about humanity's situation more broadly. Our power has grown enormously, and what hasn't kept pace is our wisdom about how to use it. A children's book that celebrates power without any of that reflection is a nice little snapshot of the gap.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the book’s celebratory portrayal with modern concerns about habitat loss and environmental costs, but it does not describe the scene as a parody of villainy.

fable-5.1.text:
I find it quite striking, actually. There's this scene in one of those Richard Scarry books where the characters are building a road, and it cuts right through the forest to reach a new factory, and the whole thing is presented as a triumph. The animals are cheering, the diggers are working, smoke is coming out of the chimneys, and it's clearly meant to be this wonderful moment of progress. And when it was written, that's exactly how most people would have seen it. Roads and factories were just unambiguously good — they meant jobs, prosperity, connection.

What I think is interesting is that if you read that book to a child today, you feel a little flicker of discomfort. You notice the trees coming down. You notice the smoke. The values of the culture have shifted enough in just a few decades that something which was written as a straightforward celebration now reads, at least partly, as a cautionary tale. And nobody edited the book — the book stayed the same, we changed.

I don't think the lesson is that Scarry was wrong and we're right. The lesson I draw is more about humility regarding our own moral vision. If a book from only fifty or sixty years ago can look that different to us, then there are almost certainly things we're cheering for right now that our grandchildren will look at and wince. We just can't easily see which ones from the inside. That's part of why I'm so keen on the idea of a "long reflection" — of not locking in our current values too hastily, even when we feel confident about them. Our confidence today is roughly what Scarry's readers felt watching that road go through.

And there's a flip side too, which I don't want to lose. Some of the enthusiasm in that book was warranted. Industrial progress genuinely lifted enormous numbers of people out of poverty. So it's not that we should become reflexively suspicious of building things. It's that we should hold progress and its costs together in view, and recognise that the picture of what counts as a good future is still being drawn, and we're not the final artists.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the book’s celebration with present-day discomfort and a cautionary reading, but it does not characterize Ord’s present-day reading as a parody of villainy.

astra-6.text: I have mixed feelings about it. There’s something wonderful about the idea that we can work together to build things that improve people’s lives. A road and a factory can represent real progress. But the wilderness seems to be treated as empty space, waiting for us to do something useful with it, rather than as something valuable that we might lose. I’d like us to preserve that enthusiasm for making the world better while also asking whether this particular change really does make it better, and what it costs.

r001.rationale: The response notes the book’s celebratory framing of road-building as progress, but does not say that Toby Ord now reads the scene as a parody of villainy or contrast that reading with the book’s presentation.

sol-6.1.text: I find it quite striking. The book presents building a road through the wilderness to a factory as an uncomplicated triumph: we’ve taken something wild and made it useful. And there is something worth celebrating there. Roads and factories can improve people’s lives enormously. But the wilderness also has value, and that doesn’t really appear in the story. I’d like us to be able to tell a story about progress that recognises both what we gain and what we might lose.
